COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY · EXPLORATORY RESEARCH STUDY · OCTOBER 2026

Predicting drug responses
across immune cell types

Can responses measured in one immune-cell context predict the effects of the same compound in another?

Main finding. The neural ensemble achieved 0.3219 mean profile RMSE, a 10.4% reduction versus predicting no change. Its advantage over a linear model with matched target compression was only 0.0013, with a 95% drug-cluster interval of [-0.0036, 0.0069]. These results do not establish a clear nonlinear advantage.

Data and experimental design

Real, public OP3 drug-perturbation measurements in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The supplied processed matrices contain 5,317 genes and four annotated cell types. Training used 306 conditions, including eight positive-control compound profiles; 96 public-validation conditions selected hyperparameters. Selected models were then refit on all 402 development conditions and evaluated on 151 official private-test conditions from 76 compounds in B and myeloid cells.

Complete drug–cell-type pairs are held out. Each test compound and cell-type label is present in development data. The outcome is estimated log2 fold change relative to DMSO; this is a study of effect-size prediction, not the competition's transformed-p-value leaderboard task. All code-fitted vocabularies and target PCA use training outcomes only.

Five model recipes, one final test

RMSE ↓ Pearson ↑ Top-50 overlap ↑ Top-50 sign accuracy ↑
model
No change 0.3592 — — 0.0000
Drug mean 0.3926 0.2466 0.1828 0.7001
Additive ridge 0.3347 0.3637 0.2305 0.7474
PCA ridge 0.3232 0.3911 0.2592 0.7597
PyTorch ensemble 0.3219 0.4044 0.2800 0.7645

The neural model is a compact one-hot drug/context network with a linear skip and nonlinear hidden layer, predicting 24 training-derived response components. Three fixed seeds are averaged. PCA ridge is a linear comparator with the same component count; it also performs strongly. Unregularized transfer of the same drug's mean response across training cell types is worse than predicting no change, showing that transfer requires care.

Reliability and biological interpretation

The neural model recovers 28.0% of each condition's 50 largest observed absolute-effect genes, on average. This describes effect-size ranking, not statistically significant gene recovery. Ensemble disagreement had effectively no rank association with prediction error here (Spearman correlation: 0.01); it should not be used as a reliable confidence score.

Reactome release 93 provides 1,042 gene sets with at least ten measured genes, covering 3,455 distinct measured genes. Pathway scores average measured gene log fold changes; they are descriptive summaries and can cancel opposing changes. Pathways overlap and coverage is incomplete. The displayed condition, Vanoxerine · B cells, was selected by proximity to the median observed response norm.

In this example, both compressed models capture the negative interferon-related gene-set means, while missing several positive calcium-associated means. These are descriptions of measured expression patterns, not evidence that specific signaling pathways were activated or inhibited.

Choosing the next experiment

A secondary offline simulation reveals measured responses from a development-only acquisition pool. Both strategies start with the same 144 labeled conditions and evaluate on the same 96 public-validation conditions. At 264 labels, design-based ridge leverage averaged 0.3634 RMSE versus 0.3660 for random acquisition over five initializations.

This demonstrates a reproducible experiment-selection loop under these conditions. Leverage is a design-based variance proxy, independent of hidden pool outcomes, and is not calibrated biological uncertainty. Public validation is reused for this descriptive study; the final private test is excluded throughout acquisition.

What the study establishes

  • Regularized response transfer improves on no-change and naive cross-context averages on these processed benchmark outcomes.
  • Low-dimensional linear prediction captures much of the observed gain. Architecture, optimization, regularization and ensembling remain different across recipes.
  • The experiment-selection simulation favors leverage at the examined budgets; generalization to other screens remains an open question.

Limits and next experiments

The original benchmark performs upstream gene filtering and parts of normalization/differential-expression estimation jointly across conditions, including test samples. This is evaluation on benchmark-provided processed outcomes, not fully isolated raw-data preprocessing. Responses aggregate donors, so donor generalization is untested. Compounds and context labels are known; new-drug or entirely new-cell-type performance is not assessed. There is no tissue geometry, explicit cell–cell signaling model, mechanistic inference or wet-lab validation.

The next stronger tests are donor-resolved, raw-data-isolated preprocessing; an external perturbation dataset; better calibrated uncertainty; and prospective experimental validation. No state-of-the-art or therapeutic-efficacy claim is made.
